_doc: Search performance budgets. `budgets` is the MEASURED record (npm run perf:search, live production data) and is documentation a human reads. `static` is the machine-enforced half: scripts/check-search-perf-budget.mjs (npm run ci:search-perf-budget) runs inside the secret-less ci:gates chain, so it cannot time a query — it enforces the structural invariants that keep the measured numbers true (ISR revalidate, fetch timeouts, cache wrappers, row caps, bounded reads). Refresh `budgets` with: npm run perf:search -- --json

measurement.environment: laptop over the public internet to Supabase project dwvlophlbvvygjfxcrhm, live production data. Vercel runs closer to the database, so production is faster than these numbers, never slower.
measurement.cacheNote: The measurement stubs next/cache so unstable_cache is a passthrough. Every timed call is a real query. 'cold' is the first run, 'warm' the median of the rest — a warm DATABASE, not a warm Next cache.
measurement.budgetRule: budgetMs is set at roughly 2x the worst observed cold time with a 500 ms floor, so network jitter and a cold Postgres buffer never trip it while a real regression (dropped index, lost cache wrapper, unbounded select) shows up as a multiple.

budgets.why: Whole-MV first page. The slowest unfiltered read, because no index narrows it before the sort.
The single most common search shape on the site. Indexed city read plus an exact count in one query.
City plus price plus beds. Adding registry filters must not cost more than the city read itself.
Ten filters across price, beds, baths, sqft, year, garage, acreage and two feature booleans, sorted by price. The all-filters sheet's worst realistic case.
PostGIS key resolution plus chunked .in() re-read. Two round trips by construction, so it carries the widest budget of the row paths.
Head count behind the live match total. Runs on every filter change, so it has to stay under a quarter second.
Same head count with seven predicates. The count must not diverge from the row read it labels.
3,808 facet rows paged out of search_facet_counts at 1,000 per page. Four round trips, cached for 15 minutes to match the table's refresh.
The shapes RPC on its own, one Bend-sized polygon returning 620 keys. Budget matches the drawn-shape row path it feeds.

knownDegraded.finding: STILL DEGRADED. The harness shape is getListingsWithAdvanced({city:'Bend', statusFilter:'closed', hasView:true}) and it still exhausts the 12s statement timeout (57014) with zero rows. Migration 20260731190000_search_advanced_deferred_join rewrote the RPC as a deferred join, which fixed the SORT-PAYLOAD half of the problem but NOT this shape, because this shape is bound by TOAST detoasting, not by sorting. No budget is assigned because the path still never completes.
knownDegraded.rootCause: listings.details is a jsonb averaging 10 KB in a 12 GB TOAST relation, against shared_buffers=1GB. Every predicate that reads details (hasView / hasPool / hasFireplace / hasWaterfront / hasOpenHouse / keywords / property sub-type / viewContains) must detoast the WHOLE document per candidate row — Postgres cannot read one key out of a TOASTed value. Measured live 2026-07-31, bounded to 5,000 closed+Bend rows: 41.1s of filter time over the row fetch = 8.2 ms/row scattered, ~15.8 buffers/row. The full closed+Bend candidate set is 96,673 rows, i.e. roughly 13 minutes. count(*) OVER () is part of the pagination contract, so the predicate cannot be short-circuited by the LIMIT. No query rewrite removes this work.
knownDegraded.whatTheDeferredJoinFixed: The base CTE no longer carries l.details or the 18 wide payload columns through the WindowAgg tuplestore and Sort; it carries only the PK plus the four sort inputs plus count(*) OVER (), then joins back to listings on the PK for the returned page. Apples-to-apples on closed+Bend limit 12 offset 3000: 4,806 ms -> 2,516 ms (-48%), and the temp-file spill (temp read=5,401 written=2,982 blocks, ~66 MB) is eliminated entirely. Row-for-row parity verified against the pre-change function across 10 argument shapes (identical rows, identical order, identical full_count).

measuredGains.closed+Bend offset 3000: legacy 2320/2678 ms -> new 2216/2261 ms (min/median, 3 interleaved runs)
measuredGains.jsonb feature shapes: no material change, as expected — detoast-bound, not sort-bound

knownDegraded.remainingFix: Eliminating the detoast needs a narrow indexed projection of the handful of details keys the predicates read, computed with the IDENTICAL expressions so semantics do not shift (the typed columns pool_yn / fireplace_yn / view_description DISAGREE materially with the jsonb — closed Bend: jsonb pool 15,763 vs typed 167; jsonb fireplace 74,148 vs typed 58,828 — so they are NOT a valid substitute). Build cost measured 2026-07-31: a sequential full-table detoast pass runs at 1.25 ms/row, so one pass over 594,141 rows is about 12.4 minutes. One narrow flags projection covers every feature predicate in that single pass; separate partial expression indexes cost roughly the same per index (double under CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) and still cannot cover the dynamic keyword ILIKE. Needs an explicit decision because a projection changes freshness semantics on a public search surface.

timeoutCeilings.name: withTimeout
timeoutCeilings.why: The split view degrades to an empty result rather than blocking the render on a slow Supabase.

timeoutCeilings.name: withTimeout
timeoutCeilings.why: Secondary fetches on the SEO search routes fail soft fast.

timeoutCeilings.name: LISTINGS_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS
timeoutCeilings.why: Ceiling for the primary listings fetch. Raising it means a user waits longer on the known-degraded RPC path.

rowCaps.name: SHAPE_KEY_PAGE
rowCaps.why: One PostgREST page. Above 1,000 the response silently truncates.

rowCaps.name: MAX_SHAPE_KEYS
rowCaps.why: Ceiling on key resolution before the search degrades to the bbox fallback. Each 1,000 keys is another round trip.

rowCaps.name: SHAPE_KEY_CHUNK
rowCaps.why: Keys per .in() chunk. Larger chunks push the request URL past safe length.

rowCaps.name: PAGE_SIZE
rowCaps.why: Facet paging step, pinned to the PostgREST cap.

rowCaps.name: cap
rowCaps.why: Viewport row cap behind the map. Every row is a marker plus a card, so this is a render budget as much as a query budget.

rowCaps.name: limit
rowCaps.why: The filter schema's page-size ceiling. Above the PostgREST cap the read truncates without an error.
